summary: Henri Seyrig was a historian and archaeologist who studied at the University of Paris from circa 1916 to 1922. He later taught Daniel Schlumberger and served as director of the Institut français du Proche-Orient from circa 1946 to 1967.
Henri d'Ollone worked in sinology and tibetology. He completed his military education at the École spéciale militaire de Saint-Cyr circa 1888–1890.

Henri de Lubac, active in religious and Buddhist studies, earned his Dr.theol. from the Pontifical Gregorian University. He taught at the Théologat de Fourvière (~1929–1950) and was a professor at the Catholic University of Lyon (1929–1961).

Indologist Henriette Johanna Wilhelmina Salomons studied at Leiden University under Christianus Cornelis Uhlenbeck (B.A. 1901) and earned her Ph.D. at Utrecht University under Willem Caland (~1906–1913). She later lectured in Dutch at the University of Copenhagen (1928–1929).

Linguist Henrik Barić studied at Graz under Rudolf Meringer and completed his Ph.D. at Vienna. He taught at the University of Belgrade (1920–1954) before becoming a professor at the University of Sarajevo and director of the Institute of Balkan Studies (~1954–1957).

Linguist and religious scholar Henrik Samuel Nyberg completed his Ph.D. at Uppsala University (1908–1919), studying under Johansson, Zetterstéen, Danielsson, and Persson. He later served as docent and professor of Semitic languages at Uppsala University (1919, 1931–1956).

Henrik Zilliacus was a scholar in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Helsinki from circa 1926 to 1936, held a post there from circa 1944 to 1974, and taught Klaus Karttunen.
Henry Alfred Whitehead, an indologist and religious studies scholar, studied at Trinity College, Oxford (~1873–1877). He served as principal of Bishop's College, Calcutta, from circa 1883 to 1899.

Henry Baily Wade Garrick, who studied at the Royal College of Art, worked in archaeology and Indology. He served as Alexander Cunningham's assistant at the Archaeological Survey of India (1880–1890) and as an artist at the Geological Survey of India (1891–1911).

Henry Beveridge, active in Indology and history and archaeology, studied at the University of Glasgow and Queen's University Belfast. He served in the Indian Civil Service (1857–1893) and as president of The Asiatic Society (1890–1891).
Henry Bower was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Vepery Seminary. Around 1857, he served as the principal Tamil examiner at the University of Madras.

Henry Chung-hung Shiu works in Buddhist studies and philosophy, holding a post at Emmanuel College, Toronto. He earned his PhD from the University of Toronto (-2006), having studied under Shek-Wing Tam, Leonard Priestley, David Waterhouse, and Willard Gurdon Oxtoby.

Henry Clarke Warren worked in Buddhist studies and Indology, co-founding the Pali Text Society and Harvard Oriental Series. He studied at Harvard, Johns Hopkins, and Oxford under Lanman, Palmer, Greenough, Bloomfield, and Rhys Davids.

Henry Cousens was an archaeologist and Indologist. He worked for the Archaeological Survey of India as an assistant to Alexander Cunningham in 1881 and later served as Superintendent of Western India from 1891 to 1910, having succeeded James Burgess in 1886.

Henry Creswicke Rawlinson worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies and archaeology after studying at Great Ealing School and Middlesex University. He served in the East India Company, Foreign Office, and as director of the Royal Asiatic Society (1862–1895).

Henry Drummond Williamson studied at Corpus Christi College, University of Cambridge (~1874–1889), earning a B.A. and M.A. Active in Indology and linguistics, he served as a missionary with the Church Missionary Society from 1877 to 1893.

Henry George Briggs was an Indologist and historian. He served as Assistant Secretary at the Great Indian Peninsula Railway in 1856, Secretary to the Bombay Municipal Corporation (1860–1862), and held a post with the Public Works Department.

Henry George Keene studied at Wadham, Sidney Sussex, and East India Company colleges. He served in the East India Company (~1798–1811) and was Professor of Arabic and Persian and Registrar at East India Company College (1824–1834).

Henry Green, an Indologist and historian, served as Headmaster of the English School, Surat (1841), Professor of Political Economy and Literature at Deccan College (1837–1857), and superintendent of the Sir Jamsetjee Jeejebhoy Parsee Benevolent Institution (1852–1854).

Henry Hamilton Hadley studied at Yale, Andover Theological Seminary, and Union Theological Seminary. Specializing in religious studies and linguistics, he served as Professor of Hebrew at Yale University (~1858–1862) and professor of Hebrew at Union Theological Seminary (1862).
